source.title: AI shares emotion with humans across languages and cultures
source.authors: Xiuwen Wu; Hao Wang; Zhiang Yan; Xiaohan Tang; Pengfei Xu; Wai-Ting Siok; Ping Li; Jia-Hong Gao; Bingjiang Lyu; Lang Qin

record.tranche_reason: Applies SAE feature extraction and evaluation to LLMs and reports results bearing on V4's indirect-evidence claim. It does not test toy-model superposition itself.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses polysemantic neurons in its introduction, but does not experimentally test feature competition, sparsity-dependent superposition, or the proposed capacity account. Its rows concern SAE-feature prediction of human affective ratings. Steering results are deliberately induced and are not treated as evidence of naturally occurring emotional behavior.
record.test_reason: The study uses pretrained Gemma Scope and Llama Scope SAEs as a tool to build 'emotion spaces'. It reports how well its own feature subsets predict human valence and arousal ratings, and how well SAE-derived vectors steer emotional tone. It never measures whether the models' activations are superposed, whether features spread across neurons, or whether SAEs recover the model's sparse features. Polysemanticity appears only as motivation in the introduction. The rows compare the study's own feature-selection sets (EN∩CH vs (EN∪CH)^C vs all), so this is T4, not a V4 test.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors also report that emotion-space geometry correlates with valence and arousal (CEBRA latent dimensions, Fig. 2e). They state the work does not imply LLM sentience.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses concept-driven SAE feature extraction, rating prediction, and feature steering; it does not use or reproduce the original toy-model superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: Prediction accuracy was lower for cross-language than within-language prediction, and valence was predicted more accurately than arousal. Results were aggregated across different SAE layers and feature widths.

fits_no_version.finding: SAE features activated by emotion concept-words in Gemma2-9B-IT and Llama3-8B-IT predict human word valence and arousal ratings within and across English and Chinese. Intersectional features are comparable to all features and better than features outside both emotion spaces.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features selected by human concept-words carry information predictive of human affective norms (interpretability utility, not superposition).

record.code_released: Upon request from the corresponding authors; no URL stated.
record.problems: The text gives qualitative comparisons but not the numerical prediction correlations shown in the figures. The results establish predictive utility of selected SAE features, not completeness, stability, canonical status, or superposition geometry of those features.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant prediction comparisons were left out. Steering outcomes were not included as rows because they measure deliberately induced emotional expression, not naturally occurring feature structure.

untested.parts: No toy models; no sparsity-dependent transition or geometry.
No test of capacity or feature-importance accounts of polysemanticity.
No test of non-capacity causes of polysemanticity.
Takes pretrained SAEs as given. It does not measure neuron spread of features, superposition, or whether SAEs recover true model features; predictive utility of SAE subsets is not evidence for these.
No test of completeness, stability across seeds or widths, or canonicity of SAE features. It uses several widths and layers but only aggregates prediction results.
No comparison of 1-D vs multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V4 'supports' label is removed. Predicting human ratings with chosen SAE subsets reports the study's own method performance; it is not evidence that models contain SAE-recoverable sparse features. Steering results are deliberately induced and were correctly excluded. Minor inconsistency: Table S3 lists Gemma widths as 16k/32k, while the text says 16k/131k.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test sparse feature storage, overlap geometry, sparsity-dependent transitions, or regular geometry in toy networks.
Does not test whether feature competition or limited capacity explains polysemanticity, or whether importance determines dedicated versus shared dimensions.
Does not investigate causes of polysemanticity or test whether it can arise without capacity pressure.

Tests whether SAE-derived features in LLMs predict human affective ratings. Does not measure how many neurons participate in a feature, establish that features are sparse in the sense used by the claim, or test superposition geometry.
Does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units of the model's representation.
Does not compare one-dimensional directions with multidimensional feature representations.

rows.subject: Gemma2-9B-IT
rows.operation_detail: Used SAE feature activations and LightGBM to predict human valence ratings; compared intersectional features (EN∩CH) with extra-space features ((EN∪CH)C).

conditions.value: across SAE configurations; 5-fold cross-validation repeated with 10 random seeds

rows.measure: Pearson correlation between predicted and human valence ratings
rows.baseline: Extra-space features ((EN∪CH)C); numeric correlation not stated
rows.value: Intersectional features had significantly superior predictive accuracy to extra-space features; performance was statistically comparable to all features. Numeric correlation not stated.
rows.uncertainty: Bonferroni-corrected P < 0.001 for feature-set comparisons; error bars are SD across 10 initializations and SAE configurations, numeric SD not stated.
rows.locator: Results, 'Emotional SAE features encoded in LLMs align with human linguistic emotion perception'; Fig. 3a
rows.note: Reported as a consistent aggregate across SAE configurations; the text does not give the correlation value.
rows.check: This compares the study's own feature subsets (EN∩CH vs extra-space) on predicting human valence. That is the paper's method performance, not a measure of SAE-recoverable sparse features or neuron spread. Numeric r is not given in the text. The baseline is another feature subset, not a control for superposition.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Gemma2-9B-IT and Llama3-8B-IT; within-language and cross-language rating prediction
reader_labels.reason: SAE-derived intersectional features predicted affective ratings significantly better than extra-space features and were statistically comparable to the complete feature set, across the reported settings (r1-r16).
